United States District Court, [Sample Jurisdiction]

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO SUPPRESS ELECTRONIC SURVEILLANCE
(SAMPLE excerpt for citation verification only. Not legal advice. Not a court filing.)

I. The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places.

Early telephone-wiretap law treated the absence of a physical trespass as decisive. Olmstead v. United States, 277 U.S. 438 (1928). Later cases still asked whether the government had occupied a constitutionally protected area. Silverman v. United States, 365 U.S. 505 (1961).

That property-only approach does not decide this SAMPLE. The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places. Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967). A person who occupies a telephone booth and shuts the door may have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the conversation even if the booth is in public view.

Later cases test the limits of that expectation. A conversation with a false friend who is wired for sound may fall outside Katz. United States v. White, 401 U.S. 745 (1971). Sense-enhancing technology that reveals details of a home that would otherwise require physical intrusion can be a search. Kyllo v. United States, 533 U.S. 27 (2001). Numbers dialed to a telephone company raised a third-party question. Smith v. Maryland, 442 U.S. 735 (1979).

Interception of wire communications is also addressed by statute. 18 U.S.C. § 2511. Warrant practice remains governed in part by Fed. R. Crim. P. 41. The constitutional baseline is U.S. Const. amend. IV.
